title: Lion
summary: The only cat that lives in permanent social groups, and a species that has lost most of its historical range.

age6_8.summary: A big cat that lives in a family group called a pride.
age6_8.body:
Lions are big cats. They live in Africa, in grassy places [1].

Most cats live alone, but lions do not. They live in families called prides [1].

The males have a thick fluffy mane around their heads. The females do not [1].

The females do most of the hunting, and they often hunt together as a team [1].

A lion's roar is very loud. You can hear it from many kilometres away [1].

Lions sleep a lot — sometimes twenty hours a day. Hunting takes a lot of energy, so they rest between meals [1].

age9_12.summary: Why lions live in groups when other cats do not, and why their numbers have fallen.
age9_12.body:
Lions are large cats native to Africa, with a small remaining population in India [2].

## The only social cat

Almost every other cat species is solitary. Lions are the exception, living in prides of related females, their cubs, and a small number of adult males [1].

Why? The likely answer is the open habitat. On grassland, prey is large and hard to hide, and a kill is difficult to defend from hyenas and other lions. Working as a group helps both to bring down big prey and to keep it [1].

## Division of labour

Females do most of the hunting, often coordinating so that some drive prey towards others waiting in cover.

Males are heavier and slower, and their manes make them conspicuous — poor traits for stalking. Their role is mainly defending the pride's territory and its cubs from rival males [1].

## The mane

Only male lions grow manes. Darker, fuller manes are associated with older, better-fed males, and lionesses appear to prefer them. The mane may also protect the neck in fights, though that idea is debated [1].

## The roar

A lion's roar can carry around 8 kilometres. It is produced by unusually shaped vocal folds that vibrate easily, letting the animal make a very loud sound without straining [1].

Roaring advertises territory and helps scattered pride members locate one another.

## Decline

Lions once ranged across Africa, southern Europe, the Middle East and into India. Today they occupy less than a tenth of that range [2].

The IUCN lists them as Vulnerable. The main pressures are loss of habitat, loss of the wild prey they depend on, and conflict with farmers protecting livestock [2].

One population of Asiatic lions survives in the Gir Forest in India — the last of the lions that once lived across Asia [2].

teen.summary: A large felid distinguished by obligate sociality, marked sexual dimorphism, and extensive range contraction.
teen.body:
*Panthera leo* is the second largest living cat and the only felid with a permanently social organisation [1].

## Sociality

Prides typically comprise related females, dependent offspring, and a coalition of one to several adult males holding tenure. Female philopatry maintains matrilineal continuity; males disperse and compete for pride tenure, which is generally short.

The leading explanation for sociality centres on resource defence. In open habitat, kills are conspicuous and subject to kleptoparasitism by spotted hyenas and rival lions, and group defence of both carcasses and territory yields fitness benefits. Cooperative hunting of large prey is a contributing but probably secondary factor, since per-capita intake does not always increase with group size [1].

Communal cub rearing, including allosuckling among synchronously breeding females, further supports the kin-selection account.

## Sexual dimorphism

Males are substantially heavier and bear manes. Mane characteristics function as signals of condition: darker manes correlate with higher testosterone and better nutrition, and both females and rival males respond to them. The competing hypothesis that manes protect the neck during combat has weaker support, and thermoregulatory costs of a dark mane are measurable [1].

## Infanticide

Incoming male coalitions commonly kill unweaned cubs. This terminates lactational anoestrus and returns females to reproductive condition sooner, increasing the new males' reproductive output during a short tenure. It is a well-documented behaviour and is a significant determinant of population dynamics rather than an aberration [1].

## Vocalisation

Lion vocal folds have a flattened, square profile with a substantial fat and collagen composition, allowing them to deform under low airflow. This produces high-amplitude, low-frequency roaring at reduced physiological cost, carrying several kilometres across open habitat [1].

## Conservation

Historical range extended across Africa, southeastern Europe, the Middle East and into the Indian subcontinent. Present occupancy is under ten percent of that extent, and the species is assessed Vulnerable [2].

Principal drivers are habitat conversion, depletion of the wild ungulate prey base, and retaliatory killing following livestock predation. Populations in fenced, intensively managed reserves are often stable or increasing while unfenced populations decline — an outcome that raises difficult questions about what conservation success means.

*P. l. persica* survives as a single population in and around the Gir Forest, Gujarat, recovered from a nineteenth-century bottleneck of very few individuals and consequently carrying low genetic diversity [2].

adult.summary: A social pantherine felid whose group living, sexual dimorphism and infanticidal male turnover are closely linked, and whose range has contracted by over ninety percent.
adult.body:
*Panthera leo* is a large pantherine felid and the only extant cat with obligate social organisation [1].

## Social evolution

Pride structure comprises philopatric related females with dependent young and a resident male coalition of variable size and typically short tenure.

The adaptive basis of sociality has been extensively tested. Cooperative hunting explanations are weakened by evidence that per-capita food intake does not increase monotonically with group size and can decline at intermediate sizes. Resource and territory defence explanations perform better: high-quality territories, particularly those including river confluences, are contested, and larger female groups retain them more successfully.

Cub defence against infanticidal males provides a further selective pressure favouring grouping. The current synthesis treats lion sociality as multiply determined rather than attributable to a single benefit [1].

## Sexual selection

Mane expression is condition-dependent, integrating testosterone status and nutrition. Experimental work using life-sized models demonstrated that females preferentially approached dark-maned models and males avoided them, establishing a dual signalling function.

The thermoregulatory cost is measurable, with dark-maned males exhibiting elevated surface temperatures, consistent with an honest-signal interpretation in which the handicap guarantees reliability. The alternative combat-protection hypothesis is not well supported by injury distribution data [1].

## Infanticide and population dynamics

Takeover-associated infanticide is a predictable consequence of the mismatch between male tenure length and female interbirth interval. Killing unweaned cubs terminates lactational anoestrus, advancing female return to oestrus by roughly eight months.

The behaviour has direct management implications: trophy hunting of pride males can induce artificial turnover cascades, and age-restricted harvest criteria were developed specifically to mitigate this [1].

## Bioacoustics

Roaring is enabled by vocal fold morphology departing markedly from the typical mammalian condition: a flat, square-profiled fold with a thick lamina propria rich in fat and collagen. This permits large-amplitude vibration at low subglottal pressure, generating source levels around 114 dB and effective communication ranges of several kilometres in open habitat [1].

## Conservation status and management

The species is assessed Vulnerable, with contraction to under ten percent of historical range and continuing decline across much of West, Central and East Africa, against stability or increase in parts of southern Africa.

The divergence is largely explained by management intensity. Small fenced reserves with active population management maintain densities near carrying capacity but require metapopulation-level genetic management to avoid inbreeding — an approach whose ecological and ethical status is debated within the conservation community.

The Asiatic subspecies persists as a single Gir population descended from an extreme bottleneck, with correspondingly low heterozygosity and acute vulnerability to epizootic disease. Establishment of a second population has been recommended for decades and repeatedly delayed [2].
